note:
Header banner candidates for /pages/our-philosophy, GRAPHITE REGISTER. Malcolm, 2026-08-27: someone working in a lab, looking at the camera and smiling, background blurred by foreground focus - then, on seeing the first round, two corrections: stick to the brand's graphite style, and show a SECOND lab worker behind the first looking into a microscope.

SUPERSEDES configs/banners/page-philosophy-lab-scientist.json, which fanned two lighting registers (bright clinical and low-key graphite) across four castings. The bright half is dropped: graphite #1A1A1A is the brand's primary ground and the dark hero register is what the rest of the store already uses. All four slots are now graphite and differ only by casting.

THE SECOND-PERSON BAN HAD TO COME OUT OF THE NEGATIVE LIST. The previous wave's negatives carried 'no second person, no group of people, no crowd' - written when the brief wanted one subject. Adding the colleague to the prompt body while leaving that ban in place would have produced a wave that quietly refused the new instruction, with a prompt that read perfectly. Same shape as the selfie waves' stale ethnicity bans. The colleague is instead constrained positively AND negatively: 'no third person, no second face looking at the camera, no sharp background figure' are new, so the second worker can never become a second portrait.

THE BOX WAS MEASURED LIVE, NOT ASSUMED. The hero is full-bleed at a FIXED PIXEL HEIGHT: 440px at 1920/1512/1440, 400px at 1280/1024/768, 375px at 390. So the visible shape runs 4.36:1 on a wide monitor down to 1.04:1 on a phone, object-fit: cover, object-position 50% 50% (this page is NOT right-pinned - the collection pages are). Publishing master is therefore 3750x848 = 4.42:1.

GENERATED AT 2.909:1 AND CROPPED, NOT EXTENDED. 4096x1408 is the widest frame every supplier can approach: it sits under gpt-image's hard 3:1 refusal, both edges divide by 16, and Seedream still delivers it at full 4K. Measured on the first round: seedream/gpt-image/flux2 honour 2.909:1, luma returns 2.69:1 and both NBP models snap to 2.357:1. The 4.42:1 master is cut from that with scripts/philosophy-banner-preview.py - no canvas extension, which is the step with four separate failure modes on this project.

THE CROP IS AIMED HIGH, NOT CENTRED. Round one asked for the head a quarter of the way down so the master could be cut from the middle of the frame. All six suppliers ignored it and put the head 5-14% down, so a centred cut decapitates the subject. Headroom is therefore now stated as a RATIO to the subject's own head height, and the crop is taken from 4% down regardless.

SUBJECT AT 0.7 ACROSS, AND THE TYPE MUST MOVE LEFT. Rendered at 1920 with the page's real headline, the CENTRED type runs x545-x1375 and a head at 0.7 across lands at x1350 - the type and the face are both asking for the middle, and no crop fixes that. Left-aligning the type into a capped column clears her completely; that is the arrangement already shipped on /pages/fine-lines-wrinkles (sm:place-self-center-start sm:text-start). Verified at render size, not on a contact sheet.

OVERLAY 45 -> 22. At the section's current 45 the banner reads as a grey rectangle - that is what is wrong with the picture on the page today, and it is a settings fault, not an image fault.

No references anywhere: no product, no packaging and no branding is in frame. Class B throughout.

LUMA GETS ITS OWN SHORTER BRIEF (`prompt_luma`), AND THE 422 THAT FORCED IT WAS NOT A REFUSAL. All four full briefs run 6104-6318 characters; Luma caps prompts at 6000 and answers a longer one with a bare `HTTP 422: Unprocessable Content` that names neither length nor content - which reads exactly like the content-policy refusals it also returns. scripts/generate-multi.py now honours an optional per-slot `prompt_<supplier>` key, so the shared brief keeps its detail for the five backends that can use it. The Luma variant is ~5.5k and keeps every load-bearing instruction - graphite ground, subject at 0.7 across, headroom as a ratio, the smile to camera, the out-of-focus colleague at the microscope, and the closing palette paragraph. Blind truncation would have cut that last paragraph off, which is where the graphite instruction lives.

slots.title: Graphite lab, woman, late thirties
slots.prompt:
A photograph of one woman at work in a cosmetic-chemistry laboratory, taken on a full-frame camera with a fast 85mm lens wide open. The picture is a wide horizontal band, close to three times as wide as it is tall.

THE WHOLE PICTURE IS DARK. This is a laboratory lit low and deliberately: the dominant tone across the entire frame is GRAPHITE - a deep, neutral, very slightly cool near-black - and she is lit against it. It is not a bright white laboratory and it is not an airy one.

SHE IS NOT IN THE MIDDLE OF THE PICTURE. She stands well over to the RIGHT, with her head about seven tenths of the way across from the left edge. The left half of the frame holds no one in the foreground at all - it is the dark depth of the room going away from the camera. There is also a clear band of open room ABOVE her head, about as deep as her head is tall, so the top of her head is nowhere near the top edge of the picture.

WHO SHE IS: a woman of about thirty-eight, north-western European, with dark blonde hair pulled back into a low practical ponytail and a few strands loose at the temples. Light hazel eyes, straight brows, fair skin. She wears no makeup at all.

HER SKIN IS REAL AND UNRETOUCHED. Pores are visible across the nose and cheeks, there are fine lines at the outer corners of her eyes and one faint line across the forehead, a scatter of small freckles over the nose and cheekbones, two or three small moles, and faint natural unevenness of colour at the sides of the nose and along the jaw. The forehead and the bridge of the nose carry the ordinary sheen of real skin. Nothing about her face is smoothed, evened or airbrushed.

SHE IS LOOKING STRAIGHT DOWN THE LENS AND SMILING. A genuine, warm, unforced smile that reaches her eyes and creases the skin at their outer corners, upper teeth just showing, lips relaxed. Not a wide grin, not a laugh, not a held pose - the expression of someone who has glanced up at a colleague she likes.

THERE IS A SECOND PERSON AT WORK WELL BEHIND HER, AND THEY ARE DEEPLY OUT OF FOCUS. A man in the same plain white laboratory coat is seated at a bench much further back, about three fifths of the way across the picture from the left edge - between her and the middle of the frame - side-on to the camera and bent forward with both eyes to the eyepieces of a microscope. Their head is down at the instrument, so their face is NOT visible and is NOT turned towards the camera. They are so far outside the plane of focus that they read as a soft pale shape with no facial detail whatsoever: unmistakably a second person working at a microscope, but never a second portrait. They are noticeably smaller in the frame than she is, they are dimmer than she is, and they do not overlap her.

HOW MUCH OF HER IS IN VIEW: the clear gap between the top of her head and the top edge of the picture is about as deep as her head is tall, and nothing of her is cut off by the top edge. The bottom edge of the picture cuts across her at the hip. Head, shoulders, chest, both arms and both hands are all in view.

WHAT SHE IS DOING: she has paused mid-task and turned to the camera. She stands at a long dark worktop that runs away from her into the left of the frame. One hand rests flat and easy on the worktop beside a small rack of plain clear glass vials; the other holds a slim glass pipette, tipped down and held loosely at waist height. Both hands are ordinary, correctly formed, five fingers each, and neither is doing anything strenuous.

WHAT SHE IS WEARING: a plain white laboratory coat, clean, well-fitted, sleeves at the wrist, worn open over a plain dark charcoal crew-neck top. There is nothing printed, embroidered, pinned or clipped on the coat anywhere, no badge and no card. Against the dark room the white coat is the second brightest thing in the picture after her face, and the weave of the cotton is crisp and readable at the shoulder.

ONLY SHE IS SHARP - THIS IS THE POINT OF THE PICTURE. The plane of focus falls on her eyes. HER eyes, lashes, brows, lips, the loose hair at her temple and the fabric of her coat are crisp. Everything behind her dissolves: the worktop a metre back is already soft, the colleague at the microscope is very soft indeed, and the far side of the room is completely unreadable - shapes, tone and light only, with not one legible edge, not one identifiable object and nothing written anywhere. What is nearest the camera at the very bottom of the frame is soft as well. Points of light far behind her open into smooth round discs.

THE ROOM, WHICH REACHES EVERY EDGE OF THE PICTURE: a modern cosmetic-chemistry laboratory kept deliberately dark. Charcoal-graphite cabinetry, a near-black slate worktop, dark grey-black walls, and deep shadow through most of the depth of the room. Far back there are a few cool blue-white sources - a strip of light under a cabinet, the pale glow of a screen turned away from the camera, light catching the shoulder of tall glassware - and because they are so far out of focus they read as soft rounded pools of light rather than as objects. There are also one or two very small copper-coloured pinpoints of light very deep in the background, no bigger than a coin would look at that distance, and nothing else anywhere in the picture is warm. The worktop runs off the bottom edge of the picture, the dark upper cabinets and dark ceiling fill the top edge, and the room continues past the left edge and past the right edge as well. It is dim but it is not murky: there is depth, separation and real detail in the shadow rather than a flat black wall, and no part of the frame is a plain flat field of a single colour.

LIGHT AND COLOUR: a single cool key light from her front left puts clean daylight-coloured light on her face and the front of her coat, with a soft shadow under the cheekbone and jaw and a soft catchlight in each eye. She is by a clear margin the brightest thing in the picture. The palette is graphite, dark teal and cool blue-white, with only those few tiny copper points. No overall warm cast, no golden light, no orange, no tungsten glow.

It looks like a real photograph of a real working scientist, taken by a good photographer on an ordinary working day.
